data.summary: The `mise` directory is a self-contained scenario definition for an image-building (aio-config gen) system: `scenario.toml` declares the metadata of the always-on L1 "mise engine" layer, while `fragment.Dockerfile` holds the concrete install steps that bake the mise toolchain manager into /opt/mise. Together they form the build-time contract that lets all other scenarios (L2 shell / L3 lang / L4 app) layer tools on top via idempotent `mise use -g` calls.

file_insights.name: scenario.toml
file_insights.summary: Declarative metadata for the mise engine scenario, consumed by the `aio-config gen` fragment resolver; it marks the scenario as category "os", tarball-installed, and `always_on = true`.
file_insights.source_summary: A TOML document declaring `id = "mise"`, `name = "mise engine"`, a description explaining that the binary, shims and redirected home are baked into /opt/mise (system path to avoid volume shadowing), `category = "os"`, `installer = "tarball"`, and `always_on = true`.
file_insights.detailed_description: This is the machine-readable descriptor that the image generator reads to decide whether and how to include the mise engine fragment. Because `always_on = true` and category is `os`, mise is baked into the L1 base layer of every built image, providing the tool-installation capability without installing any tools itself. The file is purely declarative — installation logic lives in the sibling fragment.Dockerfile.
responsibilities: Declare the scenario identity (id/name/description) for the generator
Specify the install mechanism via installer = "tarball"
Mark the scenario as always-on L1 OS-layer so it is included in every image
Document the design intent (capability-only engine, tools deferred to other layers)

file_insights.name: fragment.Dockerfile
file_insights.summary: Dockerfile fragment that installs the mise toolchain manager itself (engine only, no tools) into /opt/mise on the L1 OS layer, with extensive comments explaining the engine/tool separation refactor.
file_insights.source_summary: Dockerfile instructions plus commentary. The visible portion consists of header comments explaining the L1 always-on engine role, the rationale for splitting engine from tools, and the idempotent composability argument based on `mise use -g` read-modify-write semantics over /opt/mise/config.toml; the remainder (truncated) contains the tarball download, extraction to /opt/mise, PATH/shim wiring and home-directory redirection steps.
file_insights.detailed_description: This fragment is concatenated into the generated Dockerfile by the scenario resolver and executes the actual mise installation: fetching the mise binary via tarball, placing it on a system path (/opt/mise) so that mounted volumes cannot shadow it, and setting up shims/home redirection. Its long comment block records the 2026-09-22 granularity refactor that split the former ~1.5GB all-or-nothing `scenarios/mise` bundle (which dragged in 1.4GB of Rust) into a ~30MB always-on engine plus independently selectable tool scenarios. It also documents why no aggregation mechanism is needed: `mise use -g <tool>` is read-modify-write, so multiple fragment RUN layers merge idempotently into /opt/mise/config.toml's [tools] table.
responsibilities: Download and install the mise binary (tarball installer) into /opt/mise
Wire up shims, PATH and home-directory redirection so mise is usable system-wide
Ensure the install lives on a system path that container volume mounts cannot shadow
Remain tool-agnostic so downstream L2/L3/L4 scenarios can append tools idempotently to /opt/mise/config.toml
